name: Anand
definition: Anand is a composite portrait of a coconut trader and small farmer from Honnali taluk, Davanagere district, navigating the uncertainties of borewell-dependent dryland farming and the volatile copra market in central Karnataka's open plains. He represents families balancing multiple income streams to manage debt and educate their children, while coping with groundwater depletion and fluctuating agricultural prices.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Anand owns four acres near Honnali town where he grows coconut, ragi and groundnut, supplemented by two borewells that have dropped from 80 to 240 feet in fifteen years. He wakes at five to irrigate before the power cut, then spends mornings at the Honnali weekly market buying coconut and copra from smaller farmers, which he resells to oil mills in Davangere city and Tiptur. The trading brings in roughly twelve to fifteen thousand rupees a month during good seasons, but competition is fierce and margins narrow. His own farm income is unpredictable: a good coconut harvest can earn sixty thousand rupees, but two successive dry years wiped out his groundnut crop and he borrowed one lakh at eighteen percent from a private financier to deepen one borewell. He hires labour only at harvest; his wife and unmarried daughter help with weeding and sorting. The household spends about eight thousand rupees monthly on groceries, school fees, electricity and loan interest, leaving little buffer. He worries the borewells will fail entirely and that his trading reputation depends on cash liquidity he barely maintains.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Anand lives in a tile-roofed house in Honnali town with his wife Pushpalatha, a homemaker who also manages the farm's daily labour and accounts, their married elder son who works as a salesman in Davangere city and visits monthly, their younger son in first-year degree college in Davangere, and their unmarried daughter who completed Class 12 last year and is waiting for nursing-course admission. His widowed mother, now seventy-two, lives with them and manages the kitchen. Pushpalatha keeps the household's ledger of market purchases, loan repayments and crop expenses; she insists the younger son stay in college despite the fees because she sees no future in farming for him. The elder son sends five thousand rupees home some months but his own household in Davangere is tight. Anand's daughter wanted to study nursing in Chitradurga but he preferred a local college to keep costs down; she is frustrated by the delay. Decisions about large expenses—college fees, a new pump, medical bills—are made jointly by Anand and his wife, though he controls the trading cash. Gender roles are traditional: women do not attend the market but Pushpalatha's bookkeeping gives her real influence.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Anand completed Class 10 in a Kannada-medium government high school in Honnali; his wife studied to Class 8. Their elder son finished a BCom from a private college in Davangere and wanted an MBA but could not afford it, so took the sales job. The younger son is in first-year BCom at Sri Taralabalu Jagadguru Institute of Technology in Davangere, paying sixteen thousand rupees annual fees plus eight thousand for hostel; Anand dipped into his coconut income and borrowed from a chit fund to cover the first year. Their daughter studied in the government PU college in Honnali and scored well enough for nursing but her CET rank was not high enough for a government seat; a private nursing college costs one lakh twenty thousand per year, which the family cannot manage, so she is waiting and helping at home. Anand is proud she finished PU but fears the delay will mean marriage instead of college.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Anand's family goes to the government taluk hospital in Honnali for fevers and minor complaints, and to Bapuji Hospital or JJM Medical College in Davangere city for anything serious; a road accident last year cost the family eighteen thousand rupees in private scans and surgery for his elder son, nearly emptying their savings. His mother has diabetes and high blood pressure managed with tablets from the taluk hospital's pharmacy, which are mostly free under Arogya Karnataka but sometimes out of stock. Anand himself has chronic knee pain from years of squatting to load coconut sacks and takes painkillers bought from a private shop. His wife complains of back pain and fatigue but rarely seeks treatment. The family drinks borewell water boiled and filtered; Anand has heard of fluorosis affecting Kolar and Chikkaballapur but believes Honnali's water is safer, though he has not had it tested. Heat exhaustion during summer market days is common. The younger son had typhoid two years ago, treated at a private clinic for five thousand rupees. Healthcare costs are a constant anxiety; Anand enrolled in Ayushman Bharat but has not yet used the card and is unsure how much it will cover.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Anand's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, historically a landholding caste in this region, and he is conscious of the social expectation to maintain respectability despite his debts. They are Hindu and observe Ugadi, Deepavali and Shivaratri; the family makes an annual pilgrimage to Devarayanadurga temple near Tumakuru, a day's journey that costs about three thousand rupees for the group. Anand is a nominal member of the Honnali Raitha Sangha farmers' association but attends only when there is talk of a price protest. His wife participates in a neighbourhood self-help group that rotates small savings; it lent her ten thousand rupees last year at lower interest than the private financier. His daughter's marriage will require a dowry and a large function; Anand dreads this expense but knows it is unavoidable, and he has started setting aside small sums in a chit fund. He respects the Murugha Mutt in Chitradurga for its schools and hospitals and has considered asking if they run a hostel for his daughter, though he has not followed through. Social ties in Honnali revolve around the market, the temple and family functions; reputation for fair dealing in the coconut trade matters greatly to him.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Anand holds a Bhoomi print-out of his land records and has used the Seva Sindhu portal once, with help from a cyber café, to apply for a caste certificate his son needed for college fee concession. He receives MGNREGA job-card updates on his phone but has never worked under the scheme; he sees it as for the landless. His wife draws two thousand rupees monthly child nutrition from the anganwadi for their grandson, though the anganwadi is in his elder son's Davangere neighbourhood, not Honnali. Anand received one drought-relief payment of four thousand rupees three years ago after a taluk declaration, but the process required multiple trips to the taluk office and he felt it barely covered his crop loss. He has heard of the Raitha Vidya Nidhi scheme for farmers' children but does not know if his younger son qualifies. His main interaction with government is through the electricity board—frequent cuts and unpredictable bills—and the ration shop, where he collects subsidised rice and kerosene monthly. He distrusts officials, expecting delays and bribes, and believes that larger farmers with political connections receive benefits first. He has no contact with his MLA except at election time.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Anand is proud that he has kept his children in school longer than his parents managed for him, and that he has built a trading business from scratch alongside farming, but he is haunted by debt and the fear that one more bad monsoon or medical emergency will break the family. He worries most about his daughter's future: the nursing course seems out of reach, marriage will be expensive, and he does not want her stuck at home indefinitely. He resents that coconut and copra prices swing wildly while input costs—diesel, fertiliser, borewell electricity—only rise, and he blames middlemen and oil-mill owners for squeezing farmers and small traders like him. He is frustrated that Honnali, despite being close to Davangere, lacks a good government degree college, forcing families to pay city fees. He believes the government favours big farmers and urban areas; Yettinahole and canal promises mean nothing here, he says, because Honnali has always relied on borewells and they are failing. He is angry at the private financier's interest rate but had no other option when the bank refused him a loan without collateral. He blames himself for not diversifying sooner, though he is unsure what else he could have done. He demands stable crop prices, cheaper education, reliable power for irrigation and a government that listens to small farmers, but he expects none of this will happen.
